One of the units I was in late in my military career had this crazy, super "Hooah!" company commander. The post I was at had a lot of training grounds, so there was a lot of training to be done. Stupid training, redundant training, training for the fun of it. I liked it for the most part.

Oh, and the post commander declared no training on the weekends, so all training had to be conducted Monday - Friday. That was unheard of in the Army, but I wasn't complaining. That meant 0400 SP on Monday, and 2100 RTB on Friday.

Anyway, back to my crazy Hooah! company commander. One training week, he decides to put us through a 5 day version of what he went through in Ranger school. That meant for 5 days, we were out humping it through mountains and shit, as soon as we set up an AA and had time to go to 50/50 security, "Oh shit, we're under attack!"... The entire 5 days was like that, we got no sleep. I unrolled my sleeping bag once, just to roll it back up because "we gotta move now!". That sucked, but it was a fun suck. I hated the mountains though, 2k straightline was more like 15k up and down hill. My buddies who had been to Afghanistan were like, "If you think this sucks, imagine it by 20, because that's Afghanistan."

There was this 21 mile road our CO would have us walk down towards the training area. When it was the whole company, a release march, I was the first one up the hill to the finish. The broke dicks and supply would be at the top of the hill already setting up.

So, one day Captain Hooah! decided that he was going to have the entire company do the 21 mile road march and back nonstop. Release march. Full kit, full ruck, rubber ducks because... I guess so we didn't have to draw weapons.

So, the night before, I carb loaded, ate a lot of pasta. Trimmed my toe nails and filed the edges smooth. My boots were the most tennis shoe feeling boots that were authorized at the time, and I used those oven formed insoles. For the road march I packed a couple of these Gatorade gel packets, and a couple of BC powder packs.

The whole company started at once. I walked quickly to get to the front of the pack. A bunch of the guys at the front of the pack were jogging -slash- doing the airborne shuffle. I told them to stop that shit, that they'll just burn themselves out. Most of them didn't listen. My buddies, they knew I knew my shit though. I knew how much water I needed, and all that.

On a regular road march, I would dump out my water with 18 miles left to reduce weight. We would carry 3 qts in our camelbak and 2 - 1 qt canteens. I would keep my canteens on my back in case I needed to refill my camelbak, so they were out of my reach. Not the 42 miler, but a different field problem, I asked my buddy to hand me my canteens off my back, and I dumped one out. He was like, "What are you doing?! We don't know when we'll get water again!"... nigga please, I know my limits, give me that other canteen.

Back to the 42 mile. I didn't dump my water then. About mile 18, the guys who were trotting up ahead were burnt out. There was a stop point at the 12 mile mark and the 21 mile mark. Medics and stuff were set up there. Around mile 19 it was all uphill until you reached the top of the hill, the normal endpoint, but this time the turn around point.

At the top of the hill, my platoon sergeant was up there with the refit and rest crew. He was a broke dick, on profile... E7, 17 years in the army, no combat patch, later on accused me of faking PTSD... fuck him. Anyway, he told me "good job" when I reached the top.

Back down the hill, around mile 24, I ran into the CO, who ahead of me, and he was saying what a bad idea this was. When I reached the turn around, there were about 7 or 8 people in front of me. The CO was one of them. I passed him. I wasn't stopping at the rest points. Oh, the first BC powder I took around mile 9, I was feeling mild pain then. The second one I took around mile 26. I also took the two Gatorade gels by then.

Mile 30, I had reached the 12 mile tent. I was fucking beat. This was the first time I refilled my water. I started with 5 quarts, and took off my gear at one point to refill my camelbak. This was the first actual stop I took. At that point I was in third place in the entire company. As I was was gearing up to leave, two privates showed up at the 12 mile checkpoint. I left, and carried on.

About 2 miles down the road, 10 miles from the finish, these two privates come trotting past me. They talked shit too, those fucking assholes, "Why you so slow, old man?!"

Oh, fuck that shit, I'm not getting passed by two asshole privates! I started running.... They started running too... We all ran for about a half a mile before I just couldn't anymore. As soon as I stopped running, so did they, but they kept walking at a quicker pace than me. If I started running, so did they, they would only rest when I would, and they were in front of me... still talking shit.

About 6 miles from the finish, I couldn't even run anymore. I wanted to quit. I turned on my white light to see if the two privates were still in front of me, but they were long gone. I just kept waking. Afterwards, they told me that they saw me turn on the white light, and they thought I was right behind them, so they started running again... More on that later...

The supply and broke dicks drove by in a gator, and told me how far I was from the finish, and no one was behind me, just keep trucking... It felt like forever, that last 6 miles. I had already marched 32 miles, no problem, but I felt like I needed to just lay down. I even tried to zone out, but I couldn't, the pain in my left foot was unbearable, but I kept walking. 4 more miles, ain't that far.....

Longest 4 miles of my life. I was thinking that the next time those faggots came rolling around on the gator, I'd say fuck it, I quit, but I just kept on walking. I was hobbling at this point.

My left foot had something fucked. It felt like every toe had broken through my sock, and the fabric was tearing into the area between my toes. The last two miles I was basically skipping because I didn't want to step too long on my left foot.

I reached the end. It was pretty uneventful. 4 people had made it in front of me. Those two privates came in 1st and 2nd. They ran in front of everyone, with my help white lighting them to think I was right behind them and they needed to speed up...

Another E5 came in 3rd, and my 22 year old LT came in 4th.

As soon as reached the staging area - finish line, I was like, "medic, hydration salts now!"

"They moved everything to the halfway point, where most people dropped out."

Ok, fuck it. Took off my boots and socks.... I had a blood blister on my left foot that started on the ball, and wrapped around to the top off my three center toes. I was like, medic, you need to pop this shit. "We're not authorized to drain blisters."

Ok then... I pulled out my knife and started sanitizing it with my lighter. The medic saw what I was about to do, and was like, "Stop!! I'll drain it!"

Love medics. Fuck authorization.

He did it all sterile and proper. Wiped it with alcohol, wore gloves, and popped it with a sterile needle. It was like a runny red fluid, not all blood.

I tried to climb into my sleeping bag and go to sleep, but I was just so... I don't know the word for it, exhausted so much that I wasn't tired. I was beyond tired. I stayed up long enough for the person in 6th place to walk in. I fell asleep around then. Someone else came in 7th place, and after that, anyone still walking got picked up.

Only 7 people out of the entire company completed the 42 miles. An infantry company is ~120-140 soldiers. So it was still an accomplishment to come in 5th out of 7 who actually finished the whole thing. The CO who planned it even fell out.

June discussion of The Discovery of Witches (1647) and the Selection of July's Book Selection

The Discovery of Witches is a short read: 14 questions answered by the witchfinder general. It's a strangely defensive work. It outlines the basic English conception of witches -- in league with the devil, signing their names in the Devil's Book, feeding familiars with downright goofy names befitting Hogwarts (Pyewacket, Peckin the Crown, Grizzel, Greedigut) from "teats" impervious to pain. The description of the familiars is... eerie. They're scary, but not spectacular. Nor does Hopkins dwell on this point much. One might think that witnessing the familiars would convince a wide range of people of the reality of witchcraft, but Hopkins moves quickly to other topics.

There is some small discussion of whether these "teats" are physiological anomalies, but not much. Oddly, the familiars do not feed on the blood sucked from these teats. These are "airy" spirits and the feeding is a psychological manipulation of the witch. The use of Aristotelian elements is interesting and Hopkins outlines why witches float -- they've rejected their baptism so water rejects them. If they confess, they drown. No mention of fire.

Overall, the witchfinder seems to be more under seige than the witches. It makes me wonder how widely held a belief in witches was in 1647. The theology is pretty straightforward: the Devil has some foreknowledge of the likelihood of the witch's desires and only promises what will happen by natural means. Thus, the witch has no power, but has had his or her soul uselessly stolen by Satan through false promises.

There is a discussion of Sabbats -- occurring once every 6 weeks on Friday, not in conjunction with lunar cycles. Hopkins claim is simple: he stumbled upon "seven or eight" witches in a town near him, who met in this way. The town is named, the witches are not.

The last question is pretty cool: All that the witch-finder doth is to fleece the country of their money, and therefore rides and goes to townes to have imployment, and promiseth them faire promises, and it may be doth nothing for it, and possesseth many men that they have so many wizzards and so many witches in their towne, and so hartens them on to entertaine him.
